Ophthalmology · published research

Optic nerve injury

Several animal and ex-vivo studies report retinal-ganglion-cell survival, function, or dendritic preservation after selected red or near-infrared protocols. No human clinical outcome study is listed.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several animal and ex-vivo studies report retinal-ganglion-cell survival, function, or dendritic preservation after selected red or near-infrared protocols. No human clinical outcome study is listed.

Summary of the Evidence

Ten publications are listed in the exact optic-nerve-injury category. They comprise animal or ex-vivo work in rat, mouse, hamster, and rabbit models, with no human treatment study. One recent rat anterior ischemic optic neuropathy report and older axotomy or secondary-degeneration studies address different injury mechanisms. Chen et al. 2025

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical PBM trial or patient cohort for traumatic, ischemic, or degenerative optic-nerve injury was identified. Findings on retinal ganglion cells or electrophysiology in animals do not establish improvement in human vision, visual fields, or daily function.

Animal evidence

Rodent studies include optic-nerve axotomy, partial transection with secondary degeneration, mitochondrial optic neuropathy, and a rat model of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. The 2025 rat report used 670 nm light after injury and described improved visual-evoked potentials, greater retinal ganglion-cell survival, and lower apoptosis and inflammatory markers. Earlier studies report selected preservation of compound action potentials or axonal structure. A hamster axotomy study and rabbit injury study add different species and endpoints. These experiments vary in injury model, treatment timing, and outcome, so effects cannot be pooled as one clinical estimate.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

An ex-vivo mouse-retina study reported partial prevention of retinal ganglion-cell dendritic degeneration after 670 nm exposure. It does not test intact visual pathways or functional recovery in an animal treated in vivo.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Wavelengths include red and near-infrared light, with different exposure durations, schedules, and routes. Injury-to-treatment intervals range from immediate or early treatment to longer courses. No standard dose or delivery method is shared across the models.

Interpretation

These studies provide a preclinical neuroprotection signal, particularly for selected retinal ganglion-cell and optic-nerve measures. They do not establish that PBM restores human vision after optic-nerve injury. Controlled clinical studies with appropriate safety monitoring are absent.

Evidence strength in source summaryRetinal-ganglion-cell and optic-nerve outcomes: Preclinical signal Human visual benefit: No direct evidence
Publications and records10 publications: 9 in-vivo animal-tagged records across rat, mouse, hamster, and rabbit models, plus 1 ex-vivo mouse-retina report.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The mapped literature includes rat, mouse, hamster, and rabbit injury models, including an ex-vivo mouse-retina experiment. Several report neuroprotective changes, but models, wavelengths, and outcomes differ. No human treatment cohort or clinical trial demonstrates visual benefit after optic-nerve injury. Model-specific effects do not establish clinically meaningful recovery.

Publication and study types

  • Some reports use mixed methods.
  • No human cohort, patient trial, or clinical efficacy publication is listed.
  • Experimental cohorts cannot be deduplicated from the source records.
